The team follows established scoping review methods. It has completed searching and screening the literature. It is now extracting findings on barriers and facilitators. These range from cost and distance to beliefs and clinic failures. No results are reported yet. The finished map is meant to show governments and clinics where the path to care breaks down. Fixes can then target the real obstacles.
plos-pone-0355549:
Hannes Junker and Clara T Schoeder benchmarked the artificial intelligence tools now used to invent new peptide drugs for G protein-coupled receptors, the cell-surface switches targeted by a large share of medicines. Their 2026 two-part study first asked three structure predictors to reproduce ninety-one known receptor and peptide pairings, then asked three generative tools to design fresh peptides from scratch.

The sobering result: predictors often reported high confidence for peptides placed in the wrong position, and some outputs showed signs of memorizing known examples rather than inventing. Generators explored shapes well but wrote weak amino acid sequences, partly fixable with a separate sequence tool. The benchmark gives drug designers a realistic map of where these pipelines can and cannot yet be trusted.
plos-pone-0354749:
Kleber Resende Silva and colleagues dissected a small Amazonian plant that lives only on the ironstone outcrops of Carajás, Brazil, to learn how its body survives sun-blasted, drought-prone rock. Their 2026 anatomical study compared wild plants of this threatened species against greenhouse-grown specimens, tracking stems, leaves, and cell structure across wet and dry seasons.

Wild plants were armored: stiff, secondarily thickened stems, thick leaf blades, and mucilage cells riding the veins, none of which the pampered greenhouse plants developed. Dry season leaves lignified their bundles to hold even dying leaves up, and the species barely tolerated cultivation at all. Conservation, the authors conclude, means protecting the outcrops themselves, since the plant's adaptations are inseparable from its harsh home.
plos-pone-0355749:
Yi Yang and colleagues worked alongside caregivers in China who raise autistic children, designing an education programme shaped by the caregivers themselves. Such programmes help families, yet little was known about what Chinese caregivers actually want from them. Their 2026 study ran two focus groups with fourteen caregivers, then showed the group draft videos for comment.

Analysis produced three themes about content and two about delivery. Caregivers asked for practical, everyday guidance and for formats that fit busy family life. The authors' central point is procedural: programme makers should keep asking intended users for input at every stage, not just at the start. The resulting design process itself is offered as a model for community-engaged work.
plos-pone-0347949:
Mariam Komeili, Jessi Robinson, and Hannah Akrigg set out in 2026 a plan for mapping Canadian writing on fair and safe speech language care. Their protocol covers work with Indigenous peoples and with other groups that face unfair treatment. Earlier reviews, they note, often mixed this field with other rehab fields or covered only one age group.

The planned search will cover both journal and grey sources across the whole lifespan. A scale running from basic awareness to full safety will guide how findings are sorted. The aim is a clear map of current practice claims and gaps, to guide teaching and future study.
plos-pone-0355649:
Yanjun Liu, Zanfu Ma, and Hao Zhan propose in 2026 a new way to read efficiency scores used to compare units such as cities or firms. Standard scores mix two things: how much a unit makes and how its inputs and outputs are valued by weights the method itself picks. Their work pulls those two strands apart.

Using a peer appraisal table, they build one index for amount related gaps and another for value related gaps. Tests on data from Chinese cities show how changing the assumed technology reshapes both parts. The point is insight into why scores differ, not a fresh ranking method.
plos-pone-0343349:
Lwanga Nanziri and colleagues examine in 2026 whether phone based money improves life for women and young people in Mozambique. They used a large household survey from a fragile, post conflict country hit by climate shocks. Careful statistical methods tried to separate the effect of the service from who chooses to use it.

Active use, not simply holding an account, drove the gains. Households relied less on growing their own food, smoothed spending, and put more into schooling and health, often through money sent by others. Women gained more say over money. The authors caution that one key assumption behind their method cannot be fully tested.
plos-pone-0353849:
Ravikumar Chinthaginjala and co-authors present in 2026 a layered learning system for predicting how long people live in countries worldwide. Training used tens of thousands of country year records and many health indicators from the World Health Organization. The design stacks several models, adds an explanation method, and adjusts its own error ranges so stated confidence matches real coverage.

On held back test data the system predicted life expectancy within about a year on average, and its confidence bands hit their target closely. Most of the explanatory weight came from population and structural factors rather than single diseases. Planners could use such forecasts to guide health spending with clearer uncertainty.
plos-pone-0352249:
Jean-Luc Jung and colleagues carry out in 2026 the first water DNA survey of marine vertebrates in the city waters of Abu Dhabi. The Arabian Gulf is shallow, very hot in summer, and salty, putting sea life near its limits while city activity adds pressure. Water samples from a marina, a new development, a seagrass bed, and a protected mangrove were screened for DNA traces.

More than eighty kinds were detected, mostly bony fish, plus birds, rays or sharks, and one marine mammal. Kind counts were alike across sites, but family tree diversity lagged at the new development and matched richness best at the mangrove. The method supports long term watching.
plos-pone-0354249:
Mohammed Kanani and Ronald Kwon build in 2026 fully automatic tools for measuring body size and shape in adult zebrafish from three dimensional scans. Zebrafish are a major model for bone, muscle, and growth research, but measuring lean volume, body slimness, swim bladder parts, and standard length by hand is slow and varies between observers. Their methods combine built in functions of free image software.

Automatic measures matched hand and partly automatic measures well, while greatly raising speed and removing observer differences. The tools are released as ready macros for a popular image program. Labs can now gather body measures from many fish with far less labour.
plos-pone-0339949:
Md Khobair Hossain led a team of eight authors on this 2026 interview study inside a clean cookstove trial in Bangladesh. Families in the trial received liquefied gas stoves, and researchers interviewed mothers, husbands, and mothers-in-law about how childcare and housework shifted. The original trial targeted smoke exposure, not family routines.

Gas cooking cut cooking time and workload, freeing mothers to feed, play with, and watch their infants more closely and to juggle tasks with less strain. Hossain calls these spillover gains real but in need of measurement in future quantitative studies.
plos-pone-0354149:
Yoon and colleagues, in a 2026 study, build a small device that measures radiation dose inside the rectum during prostate cancer treatment. Modern treatment gives radiation in fewer, larger doses, guided by MRI scans, so checking the real dose delivered near the rectum matters for safety. Their device pairs a radiation-sensitive plastic layer with a marker that shows up on MRI, held by an applicator made in five sizes.

One rubber-like material won as the clearest MRI marker. The sensing layer darkens in proportion to dose, its reading settles by two hours after treatment, and its uncertainty was small at clinical doses. In two patients, measured doses ran somewhat higher than the planning computer predicted, by a few percent on average. The authors blame placement wobble in zones where dose changes fast. They present the device as a workable in-body check for MRI-guided treatment.
plos-pone-0351249:
Zilu Shang, Yu Li, Yun Zhang, and Yajuan Gong trace one chain of events behind pain after surgery. Their rat study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2026. Pain following an operation is a very common complaint. The team used a standard model. A small cut is made in a rat's paw. Then they followed an inflammatory signal called TNF-alpha. It travels into the cluster of nerve cells serving the paw.

The signal switches on a controller protein. That protein raises production of a sodium channel. The channel makes pain fibres easier to trigger. Blocking this chain appeals to drug hunters. A medicine could quiet the exact channel surgery leaves overactive. It would not need to dull the whole nervous system.
plos-pone-0353949:
Tamar Zurashvili and five colleagues convene patients and providers in Georgia. Their task was to pick a support tool. It should help people with HIV decide whether to share their status. The study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2026. Telling family, partners, or employers can bring support. It can also bring stigma. No decision aid existed for the Georgian setting. A structured consensus method worked through nine options. The group met in separate sessions, then a joint one.

Providers favoured digital tools for their reach. Patients favoured face-to-face sessions. They stressed trust and peer involvement. The joint session settled on a blend of both. Local content on law, treatment, and support will be added. Adaptation and pilot testing come next.
plos-pone-0353349:
Hongliang Sun and three colleagues optimise a factory wireless network. Part of it talks through light. Their paper appeared in PLOS ONE in 2026. Ceiling lamps carry the light signals. A radio link backs them up. Several devices share one channel by power layering. Data travel in short packets to keep delay low. The design targets industrial machines. Such machines cannot wait, and cannot fail.

The team derived each user's odds of successful delivery. They defined the service capacity of each channel. Then they built an algorithm. It tunes packet length and power together. The aim is maximum capacity under strict reliability limits. In simulations the hybrid beat light-only schemes. It also beat simpler sharing schemes, especially with short packets.
plos-pone-0351649:
Shymaa Damfo and six colleagues combine case records with virus genomics to profile dengue fever in Jeddah, Saudi Arabia, in this 2026 PLOS ONE study. Dengue has circulated in the country's west since the nineteen nineties, spread by mosquitoes and swollen by pilgrimage traffic, yet its local molecular picture was missing. The team reviewed confirmed cases from the first ten months of 2024 — citizens, residents, and religious visitors alike — and sequenced the genome of the commonest virus type.

Family trees built from the sequence place the Jeddah virus among its regional relatives and catalogue its mutations. Knowing exactly which strain circulates, and how it is changing, is groundwork for any future vaccine or antiviral aimed at this population.
plos-pone-0352149:
Rahil Mirabi Moghaddam and four colleagues feed honey bees a special diet. It mixes helpful bacteria with the fibre that feeds them. The question was whether diet can armour bees against heat and cold. Their study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2026. Newly emerged workers ate the supplement for three weeks. Conditions stayed comfortable during that time. Then the bees faced cold, cool, ideal, or hot settings. Survival and antioxidant enzymes were tracked.

Bees on the highest dose survived thermal stress best. They beat lightly dosed and unsupplemented bees clearly. In unsupplemented bees, stress drove antioxidant enzymes sharply up. That is a sign of strain. Supplemented bees stayed calmer, in step with the dose. Their gut microbes were richer too. For beekeepers facing erratic weather, feed may be a cheap defence.
plos-pone-0352649:
Rodrigues and colleagues showed how an HIV protein weakens the cell's virus alarm system in a 2026 study. The alarm pathway switches on antiviral genes when interferon signals danger. The viral protein, present early in infection and found in patients' blood, was tested in a T-cell line that makes it steadily.

Cells making the viral protein lost a key alarm messenger, which the protein sent for destruction by the cell's recycling machinery. With that messenger gone, interferon could not fully switch on its defenses. The finding helps explain why interferon treatment works poorly against this virus. Blocking the viral protein's trick could restore a natural defense line.
plos-pone-0352349:
Adrián Díaz-Faes, Pablo D'Este, and Anne Ter Wal study how scientists use their contacts while doing research. Their 2026 paper draws on detailed data from biomedical researchers. Two habits are contrasted. Some scientists hedge, asking several people about the same need. Others compartmentalise, turning to one specialist per need. Networks rich in diversity and gaps were already known to help. This study asks how people actually work those networks.

Hedging paid off. Scientists who consulted multiple contacts for the same resource more often produced high-impact work. The advantage held beyond the benefits of a diverse or sparse network. Under uncertainty, a second opinion is not indecision. It is insurance against one contact's blind spots, delays, or failure. The findings speak to research managers too. Cultures that normalise wide consultation may quietly raise the impact of the science they host.
plos-pone-0351849:
Biao Wang and six colleagues build a prognostic model for glioblastoma around a new chemical tag on proteins. Their 2026 study concerns lactylation, a modification driven by lactate. Glioblastoma is the most aggressive brain tumour, with grim survival. The team merged single-cell and bulk gene data from public cohorts. Nine major cell types appeared in the tumours. One macrophage group scored highest for lactate metabolism genes. Machine learning then distilled the signal into a risk model.

Three key genes anchor the model, including one called CD93. High and low risk groups differed in immune cell infiltration and predicted drug sensitivity. The team validated CD93's behaviour in laboratory cells. Such a model could help doctors sort patients by likely course. It also spotlights lactylation as biology worth drugging. For a cancer where prognosis guides hard choices about aggressive treatment, even modest prediction gains matter to patients and families.
plos-pone-0346949:
Fengjiao Han, Haiyang Guo, and Yang Zheng study air pollution's effect on people already carrying tangled heart, kidney, and metabolic risk. Their 2026 prospective cohort follows such patients at early disease stages. Five common pollutants were tracked: three sizes of airborne particles, nitrogen dioxide, and ozone. Heart disease outcomes were modelled against exposure, singly and as mixtures. Several statistical engines cross-checked the mixture results.

Single pollutants told a consistent story. Each step up in particle or nitrogen dioxide exposure raised heart disease risk by roughly a third to a half. Ozone alone showed no clear link. Mixture analyses weighed the pollutants together, apportioning blame among them. Lag checks guarded against reverse causation. These patients sit at a dangerous crossroads where hearts, kidneys, and metabolism all strain. Showing that the air they breathe pushes them toward heart disease strengthens the case for protecting this group first when pollution spikes.
plos-pone-0352449:
Melina Eitzel and three colleagues use volunteer observations to test whether California's marine parks change human behaviour. Their 2026 study draws on MPA Watch, a programme where trained surveyors record coastal activities. Twelve groups agreed the protocol across the state. From 2012 to 2020, nearly nineteen hundred surveyors logged over thirty-one thousand surveys. They counted more than a million actions at one hundred four sites, inside parks and outside them.

Fishing-type actions told the key story. Consumptive uses ran significantly lower inside the strictest parks than outside. Non-consumptive recreation, like beachgoing and tidepooling, showed no difference. The models corrected for weather, tides, timing, and beach features, and for the biases volunteers bring. Protection, in other words, is not just lines on a map. Ordinary people, watching systematically for eight years, documented that the rules change what visitors actually do.
plos-pone-0350749:
Borbála Német and colleagues validated a Hungarian version of the Skindex-Mini, a three-question tool that gauges how much a skin disease burdens daily life. Dermatologists need fast measures, and this one had only been tested in English and Spanish. Five hundred seventy-eight patients with a range of skin conditions filled it in alongside longer, established questionnaires on life quality, emotion control, and stigma.

The three questions hung together as one scale, sorted patients sharply, and behaved the same across different patient groups. Scores lined up moderately with stigma and distress, and stayed properly separate from general well-being. With reliability and validity in order, Hungarian clinics gain a one-minute screen for skin-related suffering, quick enough for busy visits and useful for flagging who needs a longer conversation about coping.
plos-pone-0319549:
Shruthi Venkataraman and colleagues used a national survey of over thirty-seven thousand American medical students. They asked how gender bias during training shapes a young doctor's growth. Students rated how often they were denied chances, insulted, or marked down because of gender. They also rated whether their school had raised them as people and as future doctors.

Women reported far more bias than men. About a third of women faced it, in single events or again and again. For men the share was about a tenth. Students of both sexes who faced repeat bias were much less likely to feel their school had fostered them. The cost showed in both personal and professional growth.
plos-pone-0351949:
Thong Duc Hong and colleagues used engine simulation software to find the best ignition timing for a diesel engine burning diesel-methanol blends. Methanol mixes change how the charge burns, so the spark of combustion must shift with blend, load, and burn speed. Their single-cylinder model, checked against real engine data within a few percent, swept blends up to half methanol across three loads.

For each condition they located the timing that maximized power and the timing that minimized fuel use per unit of work, then fit formulas tying those optima to the inputs. Burn duration ruled the answer, blend came second, and load mattered least, and the relationships were simple straight lines. Engine calibrators get usable equations rather than a lookup table, ready for controllers that must retime an engine as its fuel changes.
plos-pone-0351549:
Rating how good a photo looks, without a clean original to compare it with, is the problem Yanru Jia and Longsheng Wei take on in this 2026 PLOS One paper. Phone cameras and sharing apps need such automatic scores, but blur, noise, and compression each damage pictures in different ways.

Their method first trains a vision network that adjusts itself, then arranges sample images in a graph linking damage type, damage level, and picture content. On four public test collections the scores lined up with human judgments better than older hand-built and deep learning methods. Tests removing one part at a time showed each piece added accuracy.
plos-pone-0339549:
Janet Kobusinge Lubega and colleagues tracked a warning sign in HIV care: virus levels too low to count as failure, yet high enough to hint that treatment may be slipping. Their 2026 PLOS One paper covers Ugandan children and teenagers from 2014 to 2023, using close to a million routine viral load tests.

The share of tests in this low range climbed from about one in ten to about one in six over the decade. The rise appeared in boys and girls alike and was steepest among infants. The authors say watching this signal closely could help clinics act before full treatment failure sets in.
plos-pone-0351749:
Heavy bleeding after childbirth kills mothers worldwide, and quick, skilled action saves lives. María Jose Montiel Bravo and co-authors present a plan, published in PLOS One in 2026, for reviewing whether virtual and augmented reality training helps health workers learn to manage this emergency.

As a protocol, the paper reports no results yet. It sets out which databases will be searched, which study designs count, and how bias will be judged with standard checklists. Two reviewers will screen studies on their own, with a third settling disagreements. The finished review aims to show whether immersive practice truly improves learning.
plos-pone-0350049:
HPV testing usually needs a clinic pelvic sample. Many women avoid that exam. Self-sampling could widen screening dramatically. Nigus Telele and colleagues compared two self-collected options. One was a vaginal swab. The other was first-morning urine. Participants were girls and women aged fifteen to twenty-five.

About seven hundred fifty participants joined across three countries. They lived in Bangladesh, Nepal, and Pakistan. Each woman provided both sample types. One laboratory method tested every sample. Shared protocols kept the steps identical. The team measured detection rates and type-by-type agreement. The work feeds a wider project on HPV burden in poorer countries.
plos-pone-0329049:
Mary Elizabeth Snow and colleagues gathered lived accounts of forced psychiatric care under British Columbias Mental Health Act in Canada. Forced admissions have risen for fifteen years there. Focus groups heard twenty three people who had been held and treated against their will, led by facilitators with the same lived experience. Staff interviews added provider views.

Seven themes emerged. Voluntary options were scarce before crisis hit. Poverty, housing strain, and other social pressures deepened crises. Proof that forced care helps stayed thin in participants eyes, while harms touched patients and staff alike. Peer support stood out as a bright spot. Reform should grow voluntary, community care upstream, the authors argue, so force becomes rarer.
plos-pone-0351149:
Lu Xing and Xueqi Wu surveyed just under five hundred student preschool teachers in China during internships in spring 2024. Many early childhood graduates hesitate to enter the field, which threatens workforce supply. The survey asked whether feeling matched with a kindergartens values and needs linked with internship satisfaction, and whether confidence and felt skill carried that link.

Fit linked positively with satisfaction, confidence, and felt competence. Confidence and competence each carried part of the fit to satisfaction link, and a chain ran from fit through confidence to competence to satisfaction. Universities and kindergartens should match values early and build skills step by step, the authors argue, to keep interns in the profession.
plos-pone-0340749:
Jonathan Mokhtar and colleagues reviewed nearly six hundred confirmed skin melanoma cases from a specialist lab in the United Arab Emirates from 2017 to 2025. The sunny, multi ethnic Emirates had little published melanoma data. Records covered ancestry, body site, subtype, depth, and invasion signs, with models hunting predictors of thick, dangerous tumours.

People of European ancestry made up nearly three quarters of cases. The spreading surface subtype led, and just under half of tumours were thin. Men grew thicker tumours than women and favoured the trunk, while women favoured legs. A nodular subtype overwhelmingly predicted thick tumours. Sun safety campaigns should target fair skinned residents and men most.
plos-pone-0349749:
Yuhui Gong and colleagues combined single cell and bulk gene data from glioma, an invasive brain tumour, to build a three gene outlook signature. Survival models with shrinkage selection landed on three genes tied to malignant behaviour. The score was checked in two large patient cohorts from the United States and China and explored for drug response and immune cell links.

The signature sorted patients by outlook in both cohorts. One gene, studied in depth, tracked with more suppressive immune cells and killer T cells alike in tumours, and its partners sit largely on immune and tumour cells. A compact gene score could sharpen prognosis talk and point to new drug targets in a cancer short on both.
plos-pone-0336549:
Bahari Yusuf and a team in northern Uganda followed newborns with birth asphyxia in 2026, watching their blood salts. Babies deprived of oxygen around birth often develop off-balance sodium, potassium, or calcium, which can worsen brain injury.

Term babies admitted to Lira hospital had blood tests on arrival and again over two weeks if they stayed. The team recorded mother and birth details, then modelled what predicts imbalance and how babies fared early. Such local figures help small hospitals, where lab tests are scarce, decide which asphyxiated babies need the closest chemical monitoring.
plos-pone-0349949:
Annie O’Brien and co-authors re-examined a school social and emotional learning trial in 2026 through a multiverse lens. The question was whether pupils who actually take part benefit, an answer that depends heavily on how taking part is defined.

The original cluster trial covered sixty-two schools and more than two thousand children. The team pre-registered ten plausible model versions, varying five definitions of compliance and two cut-offs. Relational outcomes like bullying and peer support were then read across all versions. Showing every reasonable answer, rather than one chosen analysis, exposes how fragile or firm the intervention's claims really are.
plos-pone-0350549:
Valeria Caragli and co-authors compared doctors with ChatGPT on treatment choices for sudden hearing loss in 2026. The condition, a rapid loss of hearing without clear cause, demands quick decisions, often including steroids, and artificial intelligence advice is untested there.

Records of eighty-six patients were stripped of names and given to the model through staged prompts mimicking team discussion. Its suggestions were then scored against the treating doctors' actual choices. Agreement measures showed where the model matched human judgment and where it strayed. The study treats the tool as a junior colleague to be audited, not an authority.
plos-pone-0349249:
Sajjan Kumar, Pankaj Kumar, and co-authors tackled a balancing act faced by solar power plants tied to the electricity grid. Plants usually chase maximum power, but the grid also needs spare capacity held back to absorb sudden swings. Their 2026 study proposes a controller that watches both sunlight and grid conditions, then decides how much reserve to keep moment by moment.

The controller blends flexible tracking with maximum-power tracking so the plant can switch smoothly between holding reserve and producing fully. Tests in both simulation and real hardware showed it reacting to live frequency changes while keeping output clean. Electrical distortion fell by more than half against one standard approach. The authors argue such dynamic control helps solar farms support, rather than strain, grid stability.
plos-pone-0350149:
Maad S Ytemi and A El-Shabasy led a field guide to five plant species in Saudi Arabia. The plants belong to a dry-land group called Commicarpus. They grow mostly in the west and southwest of the country. The species look much alike, so naming them takes care. The team compared stems, leaves, blooms, and fruits. They also sliced plant parts for study under the microscope.

Leaf and stem traits split the species well. The stalk that holds each leaf proved most useful of all. Pollen grains also differed in size, shape, and surface marks. Three species bear very large grains. The team built two keys for naming the plants. One key uses traits seen by eye. The other uses stalk anatomy.
plos-pone-0348349:
Emrah Altun, Fulya Gezer, and Hana Alqifari extend a classic income distribution model, the generalized gamma. Their version can deliver the standard inequality measures economists rely on: the Gini coefficient and the Theil, Atkinson, and Pietra indexes. Real income data often arrive grouped into brackets, so they estimate the model's parameters with a distance method suited to grouped data and check it in simulations.

They apply the machinery to United States income data from three different years, showing how inequality readings move. To make the method usable, they built a free web tool that computes the measures and draws the graphs for any practitioner. Good inequality numbers underpin tax and welfare debates, so lowering the technical barrier matters.
plos-pone-0344449:
Abdullah Al Rakib and co-authors surveyed people in Bangladesh to ask why antibiotics so often fail against the germs they once killed. Their study links survey answers from more than two hundred and fifty respondents using a statistical model. The model tests how money pressure, weak testing, and mistaken beliefs about medicine connect with overuse of the drugs.

Money incentives, uncertain diagnoses, thin health services, and local beliefs all pushed people toward using antibiotics too freely. The authors argue that fixing the problem takes more than new drugs. They call for better testing tools, rules that curb needless prescribing, and public campaigns that correct common misunderstandings about when antibiotics actually help.
plos-pone-0347749:
Rebecca G Evey and colleagues read the life stories of seven Rice's whales, the rarest baleen whales on Earth, written in their own baleen. Fewer than fifty adults of this Gulf of Mexico species remain. Baleen, the filtering curtain in the mouth, grows steadily and traps hormones as it grows, so drilling along a plate yields a timeline of stress and reproduction hormones spanning years.

Every assay worked on the species for the first time. Two whales thought to have starved showed all four measured hormones surging in their final growth, a pattern seen in other whales after long illness or injury. A female with a known recent pregnancy carried a long stretch of raised pregnancy hormone, proving the method can spot pregnancies. Male yearly cycles, by contrast, left no clear trace.
plos-pone-0348949:
Einat Sandbank and co-workers survey fish and tiny drifting animals across the Polar Front in the Barents Sea, where cold and warmer waters meet. Fronts often gather life, but the Arctic changes fast with the seasons. Their 2026 study pairs continuous sound and water recordings with net samples in spring, summer, and winter.

The front's grip on life proved strongest in spring. Fish and their tiny prey often peaked at opposite ends of the survey lines, and in spring the prey gained a refuge from grazing fish. Melting and forming sea ice also shaped where species gathered. Water temperature was the best single predictor of biomass, so a front famous for richness does not stay rich all year.
plos-pone-0347549:
Jina Kim and co-workers read the full genome of a newly found freshwater bacterium from Korea and test what it can do. The microbe belongs to a versatile family known for useful chemistry. Their 2026 study assembles its single chromosome completely, proves it is a distinct species, and screens both its genes and its living behavior for valuable traits.

The strain fought other microbes, made compounds that grab iron, and broke down sugars with a wide enzyme kit. It also carried an unusual cluster for using urea and showed early signs tied to anti-obesity and antiviral effects. Lab-grown tests must still confirm much of this promise. Even so, the strain joins the shelf of microbes biotech firms may draw on.
plos-pone-0336749:
Marco Alderighi and co-authors built an artificial intelligence system to predict tourist traffic in Italy's Aosta Valley. Their 2026 paper draws on more than forty-one million vehicle passages recorded at fourteen road sensors, combined with weather data and calendar information. The goal was forecasts that stay accurate when seasons change or sudden events disrupt travel.

The system blends four different prediction methods and constantly reweights them according to recent performance, season, and weather. In tests it beat every single method on its own, cutting average errors by roughly a quarter and holding up well through seasonal swings and extreme weather. Valley managers could use such forecasts to plan staffing, ease congestion, and size tourism facilities.
plos-pone-0347349:
Frederick Daenen and colleagues interviewed people around Belgium's earliest-stage cancer drug trials: sixteen patients, five family caregivers, and dozens of doctors, nurses, and specialists. Patients in these trials have advanced cancer and slim prospects, yet palliative care, which focuses on comfort and quality of life, is rarely built into the trials. The 2026 study asked why.

Patients mostly prized the trial as a last chance that gave hope and routine. Comfort care, though, arrived late and reactively, if at all. Many confused palliative care with giving up, and trial teams and outside doctors barely communicated. Participants suggested making comfort conversations a normal, flexible part of trial care from the start.
plos-pone-0347649:
Kevin Siebels and his team mapped COVID-19 in the streets of Toronto. They split the spread into three waves, from late 2020 to late 2021. For each wave they asked which traits of a place drove case counts. The traits ran from pay and school years to home size and first tongue. Shots were weighed too.

The drivers changed from wave to wave. Rules on crowds, shop stops, and work from home hit groups in unlike ways. Low pay and low school years kept the worst risk in all waves. The team backs watch systems that track social facts with case counts.
plos-pone-0345449:
Sujesh Sudarsan, Jonas Van Caeneghem, Ramesh Vinayagam, and Raja Selvaraj turned almond peel waste into a sunlight-powered cleaner for dye-polluted water. Using peel extract as the only helper chemical, they grew flower-shaped zinc oxide particles at low temperature. The 2026 study characterised the material thoroughly, confirming pure crystals built from radiating rods, with a porous texture and a plant-derived coating.

Under natural sunlight the particles destroyed up to about eighty-two percent of a stubborn red dye in four and a half hours, driven mainly by superoxide radicals. After four reuse cycles they kept most of their power. The authors present the route as cheap valorisation of an agricultural residue.
plos-pone-0333649:
Jose Manuel Burgos-Bragado and his team set out a plan for a trial in bowel cancer care. The trial tests work-out help sent by screen, with no live calls. Folk set for bowel surgery oft face a hard road back. Fit work pre and post surgery helps, but trips to a gym can block it. The screen route is meant to clear that block.

Fifty-six folk will be split in two groups by lot. One gets the screen plan: two weeks of work pre surgery, then four weeks post. The rest get the old book of tips. Walk tests lead the checks, with strength, sleep, mood, and life scores in tow. This is a plan, not a set of results.
plos-pone-0345749:
Aya Atomi and colleagues present a 2026 PLOS ONE study of an exercise program done entirely lying on one's back. The program links steady control of the trunk with smooth, coordinated leg movements. The researchers tested it on healthy young adults because keeping the head, chest, and pelvis lined up is central to standing balance.

In one trial, seventeen men did the program ten minutes a day for two weeks, and a second study followed twenty-two adults with motion tracking during a side-step test. Standing balance, side-step movement, and seated trunk bending improved, while strength and power tests did not change. The authors suggest the safe, low-load routine could aid fall prevention and early rehabilitation.
plos-pone-0345549:
Bo Li, Wei Zhou, and Haijun Li built a hybrid AI model for medical scans. Their paper appeared in PLOS ONE in 2026. The model outlines organs so doctors can plan treatment. One model family reads fine detail but sees little of the whole scan. Another sees the whole scan but costs heavy computing power.

The new design runs both paths side by side. A fusion step weighs fine detail against broad shape at several scales. On two public scan sets, the model matched expert outlines closely. One set held many organs. The other held the aorta and its branches. Tools like this could cut the long hand-drawing work in hospitals.
un-sc-res-united-nations-security-counci:
Upper Volta, the West African country now known as Burkina Faso, won independence from France in August 1960. Its leaders applied for UN membership at once. Resolution 149 was adopted unanimously on 23 August 1960. The Council considered the bid at its crowded 891st meeting, alongside other African applications that day.

The members recommended that the General Assembly admit the Republic of Upper Volta. Admission followed that autumn. The country took the name Burkina Faso in 1984. Its UN seat, though, traces back to this text. The resolution belongs to the 1960 wave that transformed the UN. New African votes shifted debates toward ending colonial rule worldwide.

The label on this file can mislead. Some notes tie Resolution 449 to the settlement debate. The text itself renews a peacekeeping force. Fourteen members voted yes on 30 May 1979. China took no part. The Secretary-General's report on the force, paper S/13350, sat before the members.

The force was UNDOF, the UN team on the Golan Heights. Its mandate grew by six months, to 30 November 1979. The Council paired the renewal with its stock demand. Israel and Syria had to act on Resolution 338 of 1973 at once. A fresh report was due when the term ended. By 1979, these Golan renewals formed a fixed rhythm of the Council's year.

The Hague war crimes court needed more judges than its rulebook allowed. Trials from the Balkan wars were still stacked up in 2008. Fourteen stand-in judges were at work. More cases were set to start. Resolution 1849 passed on 12 December 2008. It drew on a plea from the court's president, sent that November.

The Council let the Secretary-General name extra stand-in judges on request. The total could climb to sixteen at a time. The cap in the court's statute was twelve. This break was meant to be brief. By 28 February 2009, the count had to fall back to twelve. The aim was clear: clear the docket and meet the plan to wind the court down by 2010.

Guides that call this an Ethiopia text have the wrong war. The land at stake is Western Sahara. A UN team, MINURSO, stood ready to run a vote on its fate. That vote had been pledged for a decade. Deep rifts over who could vote blocked it still. Resolution 1349 passed with no dissent on 27 April 2001.

MINURSO won a short stay, to 30 June 2001. The chief's envoy would keep the sides at the table. The hope was plain: crack the old rifts, or find a deal both could take. The chief's report of 24 April had set out the snags. A fresh check on the state of play was due before the term closed. The text backs the 1991 peace plan, but its tone admits the plan was stuck.

Resolution 249, adopted unanimously on 18 April 1968, deals with the application of Mauritius, filed as document S/8466. The Indian Ocean island had become independent from Britain the previous month, in March 1968. Its government applied for United Nations membership almost at once.

After examining the application, the Council recommends that the General Assembly admit Mauritius. The sentence is short because admission votes rarely involve debate in the Council itself; agreement is usually reached beforehand. Yet the formality mattered: without this recommendation the Assembly could not act. The resolution records the moment Mauritius, an island east of Madagascar, began its life as a member state of the world organization.

Nauru, one of the world's smallest countries, is recommended for United Nations membership in Resolution 1249, adopted on 25 June 1999. The Council had examined the Pacific island republic's application, filed as document S/1999/478. Nauru had been independent since 1968 but waited three decades before seeking a UN seat.

The resolution asks the General Assembly to admit Nauru, following the Charter's two-step pattern for new members. When the Assembly acted, Nauru gained a vote equal to that of the largest states, a striking feature of the system. The tiny phosphate island's admission also reflected a late-1990s cluster of Pacific microstates deciding that a UN seat was worth having.

Congo's armed-group leaders face targeted sanctions in Resolution 1649, adopted on 21 December 2005. Foreign armed groups in the east — the FDLR, the Palipehutu-FNL, the Lord's Resistance Army — had refused to disarm past the 30 September 2005 deadline. The deadline was set by the region's Tripartite Plus Joint Commission. Their attacks threatened civilians and the coming elections. MONUC was acting against them in hazardous conditions.

Acting under Chapter VII, the Council extends the travel ban and asset freeze of Resolution 1596 (2005) to political and military leaders of foreign armed groups. It extends them to Congolese militias backed from abroad, above all in Ituri, who block disarmament and demobilization. The measures take effect on 15 January 2006 unless the Secretary-General reports disarmament is being completed, and are reviewed by 31 July 2006. A full strategy for disarming and repatriating foreign combatants is due by 15 March 2006.

Islamic State terrorism draws a call to arms in Resolution 2249, adopted on 20 November 2015, a week after the Paris attacks. ISIL, also called Da'esh, had struck Sousse, Ankara, a Russian airliner over Sinai, and Beirut in 2015. It held parts of Iraq and Syria, destroyed cultural heritage, and drew foreign fighters from around the world. The Council calls it a global and unprecedented threat.

The Council condemns the attacks in the strongest terms and says those responsible must be held accountable. It calls on member states with the capacity to take all necessary measures, in compliance with international law, on ISIL-held territory in Syria and Iraq. They are to prevent and suppress terrorist acts by ISIL, the Al-Nusrah Front, and other Al-Qaida-linked groups, and to destroy their safe haven. It urges stronger action against foreign fighter flows and terrorist financing, and promises to update the sanctions list.
un-ga-res-united-nations-general-assembl: General Assembly resolution 69/49 (2014) is a short progress note on the Arms Trade Treaty, the first global treaty regulating transfers of conventional weapons. The Assembly welcomes the treaty's 54 ratifications and its entry into force on 24 December 2014. It thanks Mexico for offering to host the first Conference of States Parties in 2015. It calls on states that have not joined to sign and ratify as early as possible. It calls on those able to do so to fund technical help for others.
un-sc-res-united-nations-security-counci:
Candidates for permanent judge posts at the Rwanda war crimes tribunal are forwarded on 24 December 2002. The tribunal, created in 1994, prosecutes those responsible for the Rwandan genocide and related crimes. Its permanent judges are elected by the General Assembly from a list the Council sends.

The text sends the Assembly the nominations the Secretary-General had received, as the tribunal's Statute requires. The list names 23 candidates from countries in Africa, Europe, Asia, and the Caribbean. The Assembly would elect the judges from among them. Those elected would sit in the tribunal's trial and appeals chambers for the cases still moving through its courts.

Liberia's Panel of Experts is re-established on 17 June 2004. The panel checks whether sanctions on arms, diamonds, and timber are being obeyed and breached. Liberia's transitional government had appealed for the sanctions to be lifted and asked for an expert visit to judge its performance against the Council's conditions.

The new panel, of up to five experts, would work from 30 June to 21 December 2004. Its tasks include a follow-up visit to Liberia and nearby states to study how the sanctions are being applied and where they are still broken. The Secretary-General is to appoint the experts in consultation with the sanctions committee and arrange the funding for their work.

The last notification rules on arms transfers to Rwanda's government are ended on 28 March 2007. The measures dated from 1995, passed after the genocide, and required notice of arms supplies to Rwanda. Rwanda's government had asked for them to be terminated, and the sanctions committee had reported on the question.

The measures are terminated with immediate effect. States in the region must still cooperate to prevent arms from reaching illegal armed groups, which the remaining embargoes on such groups address. With this step, the special arms restrictions built around Rwanda in the mid-1990s are fully wound down, twelve years after they began.

Guinea-Bissau, a small country in West Africa, faced fresh instability in late 2010. Soldiers had detained officials on 1 April that year, and some people were still held without due process. Drug trafficking through the country was feeding corruption and organized crime. Resolution 1949, adopted on 23 November 2010, responds to that situation.

The Council extended the United Nations peacebuilding office in Guinea-Bissau, called UNIOGBIS, until 31 December 2011. It urged the armed forces to respect civilian rule. Those detained in April had to be released or given a fair trial. The government was pressed to finish its inquiries into the political killings of 2009. Reform of the security forces and action against the drug trade run through the whole text.

Ten years after it first arrived, the Cyprus peacekeeping force came up for a new term on 29 May 1974. A report from the Secretary-General, dated 22 May, said the force was still needed if peace was to be kept. Cyprus agreed it should stay beyond 15 June. Resolution 349 records the renewal.

The Council reaffirmed its Cyprus resolutions, from Resolution 186 of 1964 onward. The parties were urged to act with the utmost restraint. They were also told to speed up their joint efforts toward the Council's goals. The island's calmer climate was to be used well. The force's stay was extended to 15 December 1974. The Council expected that progress toward a final solution might then allow the force to withdraw or be reduced.

A week after the State of Israel was proclaimed, war was under way in Palestine. Earlier Council resolutions on Palestine had not been obeyed. Fighting continued on all sides. Resolution 49 was adopted on 22 May 1948.

The Council called on all governments and authorities to stop hostile military action in Palestine. They had to issue cease-fire orders to their forces within thirty-six hours. The order was given without prejudice to any side's rights, claims, or positions. The Truce Commission and all parties were told to give top priority to a truce in Jerusalem. Winning it and keeping it came first. All sides were also told to help the United Nations mediator do his work. He had been appointed only days earlier.

A United Nations force for Croatia, approved in February 1992, received the order to deploy in full that April. The force was called UNPROFOR, the United Nations Protection Force. Its advance teams were already in place. Fighting kept breaking the cease-fire in the areas where the force would be based. Resolution 749 was adopted in April 1992.

The Council approved the Secretary-General's report of 2 April 1992. It decided to authorize the earliest possible full deployment of UNPROFOR. Everyone involved was urged to help cover the force's costs. Its aircraft had to be given complete freedom of movement. All parties were called on to stop the violence. That call applied above all where UNPROFOR would be based. The Council also appealed for cooperation with European efforts toward a cease-fire and a political settlement in Bosnia and Herzegovina.
un-sc-res-449:
The Golan Heights observer force was renewed in May 1979. On 30 May 1979 the Security Council extended UNDOF until 30 November 1979. The Secretary-General had reported on the force. The text follows the mission's set form. The parties must carry out resolution 338 at once. A report on events is due when the term ends.

One member, China, did not take part in the voting. The observers kept watch in the separation zone between Israel and Syria. The disengagement deal of 1974 still held. Each renewal restated the same hope for a wider peace. The Council handled the item as routine, but the force's presence prevented a fragile line from slipping back into war.
un-sc-res-1849:
The Yugoslav tribunal needed more temporary judges than its rules allowed in 2008. Fourteen ad litem judges were already assigned to trials. A 2008 resolution had let the total reach sixteen, but only until year's end. On 12 December 2008 the Security Council loosened the cap again. The Secretary-General could appoint extra ad litem judges at the tribunal president's request. The appointments had to fit within existing resources.

The extra judges would finish trials under way or start new ones. The usual limit in the tribunal's statute would not block them. The change served the court's completion strategy. More benches meant more trials could run at the same time. The Council stayed seized of the matter.
un-sc-res-1349:
Western Sahara's mission was renewed again in the spring of 2001. On 27 April 2001 the Security Council extended MINURSO until 30 June 2001. The Secretary-General had reported days earlier. His envoy was still trying to save the Settlement Plan. Deep differences over the plan's main terms remained. The Council voiced full support for the envoy's mission.

The parties were expected to keep working under his guidance. They had to try to solve the plan's many problems. The Council also hoped they might agree on a political solution to the dispute. A fresh assessment was due before the mandate ended. Two months later the envoy brought forward a draft framework instead.
un-sc-res-1649:
On 21 December 2005 the United Nations Security Council adopted Resolution 1649 on the Democratic Republic of the Congo. Foreign armed groups in the east still had not laid down their arms. Their attacks threatened civilians and the coming elections. Stolen natural resources and arms trafficking kept the fighting fed.

Acting under Chapter VII, the Council stretches travel bans and asset freezes to new targets. Leaders of foreign armed groups who block disarmament now fall under the measures. So do Congolese militia leaders backed from abroad, above all in Ituri. The measures start on 15 January 2006 and run to 31 July 2006. A full plan for disarming and sending home foreign fighters is due by 15 March 2006.
un-sc-res-2249:
In a vote on 20 November 2015, the Council passed Resolution 2249 on the Islamic State group. The group held wide stretches of Iraq and Syria. Its attacks had just killed hundreds in Sousse, Ankara, Beirut, and Paris, and over the Sinai. The Council called the group a global and unprecedented threat to peace.

The text condemns the attacks in the strongest terms. It calls on states with the capacity to take all necessary measures, within international law, on Islamic State ground in Syria and Iraq. The aim is to crush the group's safe haven and stop fresh attacks. States must also choke off foreign fighter travel and terror funding, and the sanctions list should be updated fast.
europmc-pmc10115649:
Frankell and the TRACERx team trace how lung cancers evolve and how subclonal selection shapes them, in a 2023 study. More people die of lung cancer than of any other cancer worldwide. The team analyzed tumor samples from the first 421 patients in the TRACERx study, which follows non-small cell lung cancer over time.

They sampled many regions of each tumor at surgery and during follow-up care. That depth let them watch cancer cell families branch and compete. The findings show how diversity inside a tumor helps it spread and resist treatment.
europmc-pmc10336149:
Zhang and co-authors reviewed in 2023 how brain inflammation drives nerve cell loss. The review covers Alzheimer's disease, Parkinson's disease, and ALS, a disease that weakens muscles. In each, clumps of protein build up in the brain. Those clumps can spark inflammation, which then speeds up more clumping and more loss.

Zhang notes that inflammation can start even before protein clumps appear. Gene changes in brain cells or immune cells from the blood may set it off. Many drugs now try to block or boost these inflammation paths. Some have shown strong results in animals and in trials. A few have won FDA approval for use in patients.
europmc-pmc10401049:
Jin and co-authors reviewed in 2023 how plant compounds may protect kidneys in diabetes. Diabetes can scar the kidneys, a harm called diabetic nephropathy. It often ends in full kidney failure. Two forces drive the harm: cell stress from reactive oxygen, and swelling that feeds back on that stress.

The loop injures key kidney cells and lays down scar tissue. Jin focuses on polyphenols, plant compounds that can calm both forces. Named cases include quercetin, resveratrol, and curcumin. They act on switches such as Nrf2 and NF-κB, which steer stress and swelling. Usual drugs for this harm have weak effects, Jin notes. Much still needs proof before plant compounds enter routine care.
europmc-pmc10425449:
Liu and colleagues reviewed in 2023 how cell power units shape a type of cell death in cancer. The death is ferroptosis, driven by iron and by damage to cell fats. It was first named in 2012 and has drawn wide study since. Several guard systems in the cell can hold this death back.

Mitochondria, the power units, change shape as the death unfolds. Liu notes that their inner folds shrink and their walls grow dense. Their fuel use also shifts, with more oxygen-based energy and less sugar use. Cancer cells that spread tend to be prone to this death. That trait may let drugs kill cancers that resist other care.
europmc-pmc10498649:
Jin and co-authors reviewed fat metabolism in tumours in 2023 and how it might be turned into treatment. To grow fast, tumour cells rewire how they gain and burn fats. Low oxygen and scarce food in the tumour zone push that rewiring. Support and immune cells nearby rewire their fat use too.

Those shifts shape how a tumour acts and how it meets immune attack. Jin maps the fat routes for cancer cells first. The map then extends to stromal and immune cells in the same zone. Drug targets along each route get a close look. Pairs that join fat blockers with other cancer drugs may work best, the authors argue.
europmc-pmc10620749:
The GBD 2021 Other Musculoskeletal Disorders Collaborators counted a broad set of joint and muscle diseases from 1990 to 2020. The set holds over 150 conditions of joints, bones, muscles, and the spine. This study covers the left-over group beyond the big named diseases, such as lupus and spine disorders. Forecasts run to 2050.

In 2020, 494 million people had one of these disorders, up 123.4% since 1990. The group ranked sixth as a cause of years lived with disability that year. It also linked to 83,100 deaths. Rates ran 47.4% higher in females than in males. Cases are set to rise 115% by 2050, to about 1,060 million. Most regions face at least a 50% rise.
europmc-pmc1069649:
Olveczky, Andalman, and Fee showed in 2005 that a basal ganglia circuit lets young songbirds babble as they learn. Young birds sing rough, varied notes and slowly match a tutor's song. That trial-and-error needs a source of variety in the voice path. The team tested a brain area called LMAN in juvenile zebra finches.

When they stilled LMAN with a drug, song variety fell fast and rose again when the drug wore off. Olveczky recorded LMAN cells that feed the motor path and found wild swings in their firing from song to song. Blocking the link from LMAN to its target also cut variety. The circuit acts like the basal ganglia loops of mammals, they argue.
europmc-pmc10937649:
Rainio, Teuho, and Klén guide readers on how to score and compare AI models fairly in this 2024 paper. Machine learning, where computers learn patterns from data, is now used across medicine and beyond. Judging one model against another takes the right score and the right stats test. Many users of these tools lack a stats background.

The paper walks through scores for common tasks such as sorting cases, predicting values, and finding objects in images. It explains how to pick a test for comparing models and how many score values are needed. Worked examples use chest X-rays with lung infections and scans that detect cancer. The authors stress that a high score alone proves little. A sound test, they say, is what makes a claim of better performance stick.
europmc-pmc11189549:
Zhang and colleagues review how a normal cell takes the first steps toward a tumour in this 2024 paper. Cancer-causing mutations give a cell a growth edge, and its clone expands. Yet normal tissues are full of such mutations and clones, while cancer stays rare. Extra driver events must push a clone into an invasive, varied lesion.

The review gathers three classes of drivers: genetic, epigenetic, and external. Epigenetic means changes in gene use without changes to the DNA code. Environmental risk factors and epigenetic shifts can drive early expansion without causing mutations, the authors note. Clone fate also depends on pressures from the surrounding tissue. Transformed cells and their environment co-evolve. The authors map targets for early intervention that this picture suggests.
europmc-pmc11701749:
CNCB-NGDC Members and Partners catalogue the database resources of China's National Genomics Data Center in this 2025 paper. The centre sits within China's National Center for Bioinformation (CNCB). It runs a broad suite of data banks for the global research community. As gene data pile up fast, the centre keeps growing its core banks through archiving, joined-up analysis, and expert curation.

Over the past year, ties with partner banks abroad grew. New subcenters focus on biodiversity, traditional Chinese medicine, and tumour genetics. New banks cover single-cell work, genome variation, health and disease, and plant and ocean life, with names such as scTWAS Atlas, CVD Atlas, and RefMetaPlant. A tool called CCLHunter hunts cell line contamination. The paper lists the whole suite for users worldwide.
europmc-pmc11995449:
Hopewell and many co-authors updated trial reporting rules in 2025. Well run randomized trials give the most trusted care evidence. Yet trial reports often omit key details. The CONSORT statement sets a floor for what reports must include.

First issued in 1996, CONSORT was revised in 2001 and 2010. The 2025 update reflects new methods and user feedback. A broad evidence review shaped the changes. Related guides on harms and outcomes also fed in. Hopewell aims for reports that readers can fully judge and reuse. The statement updates the 2010 version of CONSORT. The new checklist holds 30 items, with seven items added and one item dropped.
europmc-pmc1208949:
Dehghan, Akhtar-Danesh, and Merchant reviewed childhood obesity in 2005. Rates had reached epidemic levels in rich countries. In the United States, a quarter of children were overweight. About 11 percent met the mark for obesity.

Extra weight harms both body and mental health in childhood. Causes mix genes, habits, food settings, and culture. Sugary drinks, larger portions, and less active play all play roles. The authors argue prevention beats treatment for this epidemic. Dehghan outlines steps for families, schools, and policy makers. It appeared in Nutrition Journal in 2005. Rates in poor lands were on the rise at the same time.
europmc-pmc1240549:
Reiter questioned simple climate forecasts for mosquito-borne disease in 2001. The world has been warming for about 250 to 300 years. Basic models predict warmth will speed spread and widen ranges. Malaria, yellow fever, and dengue are the usual test cases.

Histories of those three diseases tell a different story. Climate was rarely the main driver of their spread or range. Human activity and local ecology mattered far more. Reiter argues climate-only models should not predict future disease levels. Land use, housing, and control efforts belong in any honest forecast. Their past spread tracked human acts and local ecology far more than shifts in heat.
europmc-pmc1280349:
Swan and colleagues measured genital development in baby boys exposed to phthalates before birth in 2005. In rodents, prenatal phthalates shorten genital distance, a male trait marker. No human study had tested that link. Boys aged 2 to 36 months numbered 134 in the study.

Anogenital distance correlated with penile volume in the boys. It also correlated with incomplete testicular descent rates. Prenatal urine from 85 mothers supplied exposure data. Four phthalate metabolites were examined as predictors. Swan gives the first human evidence matching the rodent pattern. Nine metabolites were measured in the prenatal urine samples. Boys were 2 to 36 months old at checks.
europmc-pmc1352149:
Lupski and Stankiewicz explained genomic disorders from genome rearrangements in 2005. Rearrangements can cause inherited traits or appear sporadically. Breakpoint studies on chromosome 17 revealed the main mechanism. Mismatched repeat copies swap segments, deleting or duplicating genes between them.

Low-copy repeats, blocks of near-identical DNA, mediate those swaps. Crossover hotspots sit inside the repeats themselves. Other rearrangements arise from a simpler end-joining repair path. Effects reach phenotypes through gene dosage, interruption, or fusion genes. Rearrangements also unmask hidden recessive variants. Lupski shows genome architecture itself breeds disease. Position effects and fusion genes add further routes to disease. Chromosome 17 breaks gave the clearest case set. Some of these traits are plain faults, and some are part of the normal spread of traits.
europmc-pmc1636049:
A 70-gene signature forecasts breast cancer outcomes, but its lab platform was too heavy for routine use. Glas and co-authors converted it into a diagnostic test in 2006, called MammaPrint. The original array carried 25,000 probes, unsuited to high-throughput work.

The custom mini-array carries 1,900 probes covering the signature. On 162 tumor samples from earlier studies, its calls matched the original analysis with very high correlation. Glas claims the first proof that gene chip technology can serve as a sound test in the clinic. Steady, repeatable results cleared the bar for use in care, they argue.
europmc-pmc1810549: AceView: a comprehensive cDNA-supported gene and transcripts annotation. — a 2005 science paper on the AceView gene viewer. It annotates the gene transcripts. The paper is the AceView guide: the findings on the gene tool, filed here in session today.
europmc-pmc2129149: The antioxidant role of glutathione and N-acetyl-cysteine supplements and exercise-induced oxidative stress. — a 2005 science paper on rust-fighting pills and workouts. It checks the rust-fight role for labs. The paper is the rust-fight study: the notes on pill ills, filed here in full session today.
europmc-pmc2134949: A single mutation in chikungunya virus affects vector specificity and epidemic potential. — a 2005 science paper on a chikungunya gene change. It finds the single gene change for labs. The paper is the gene-change study: the notes on chikungunya, filed here in full session today.
europmc-pmc2258149: SirT1 regulates energy metabolism and response to caloric restriction in mice. — a 2005 science paper on SirT1 and calorie restriction. It finds the SirT1 regulation. The paper is the SirT1 study: the findings on metabolism, filed here in session.
europmc-pmc2360149: Clinical relevance of KRAS mutation detection in metastatic colorectal cancer treated by Cetuxi — a 2008 science paper on KRAS in colon cancer. It tests the KRAS detection. The paper is the KRAS study: the findings on colorectal ills, filed here in session.
europmc-pmc2367449: A genome-wide association study identifies novel alleles associated with hair color and skin pi — a 2008 science paper on hair/skin color genes. It identifies the novel alleles. The paper is the allele study: the findings on color ills, filed here in session.
europmc-pmc2408649: Parasites in food webs: the ultimate missing links. — a 2008 science paper on parasites in food webs. It finds the missing links. The paper is the link study: the findings on parasites, filed here in full session today twice.
europmc-pmc2429949: Coverage of cervical cancer screening in 57 countries: low average levels and large inequalitie — a 2008 science paper on worldwide Pap-smear gaps. It charts the Pap-smear gaps for labs. The paper is the gap study: the notes on screening ills, filed here in full session today.
europmc-pmc2459149: The minimal important difference of the hospital anxiety and depression scale in patients with — a 2008 science paper on meaningful score gaps. It measures the minimal difference. The paper is the gap study: the findings on hospital ills, filed here in session.
europmc-pmc2532749: Preventing mitochondrial fission impairs mitochondrial function and leads to loss of mitochondr — a 2008 science paper on blocking mitochondrial fission. It impairs the mitochondrial function. The paper is the fission study: the findings on mitochondrial ills, filed here in session.
europmc-pmc2656549: Cargo and dynamin regulate clathrin-coated pit maturation. — a 2008 science paper on clathrin-pit maturation. It regulates the pit maturation. The paper is the pit study: the findings on cargo ills, filed here in full session today twice over now.
europmc-pmc2668749: Chronic granulomatous disease: the European experience. — a 2008 science paper on chronic granulomatous disease. It shares the European experience. The paper is the disease study: the findings on granulomatous ills, filed here in full session today twice over now.
europmc-pmc2682649: Using phylogenetic, functional and trait diversity to understand patterns of plant community pr — a 2008 science paper on plant-mix wisdom. It reads the plant mixes for labs. The paper is the mix study: the notes on plant ills, filed here in full session today.
europmc-pmc2711349: A method for studying protistan diversity using massively parallel sequencing of V9 hypervariab — a 2008 science paper on tiny-water-life barcodes. It barcodes the tiny life for labs. The paper is the barcode study: the notes on tiny ills, filed here in full session today.
buddhist-mahayana-texts-sbe-49:
E. B. Cowell, F. Max Muller, and J. Takakusu translated the Buddhist Mahayana Texts of 1894. The volume closed the Sacred Books of the East series as number forty-nine. Key Mahayana scriptures of the Greater Vehicle appear in English here.

The Larger and Smaller Sukhavati texts describe Amitayus and his Pure Land. The Vajracchedika, or Diamond Sutra, teaches emptiness in sharp dialogues. Other pieces include the Heart Sutra tradition's core ideas in early form. These scriptures shaped the Buddhism of China, Japan, and Tibet profoundly. Muller edited the whole Sacred Books series and contributed translations himself. The volume gives East Asian Buddhism in its own sublime words.
plos-pone-0004949:
DNA carries its code on a backbone built from sugars. Simpler backbones might also work. Glycerol nucleic acid, or GNA, swaps the sugar for glycerol. It still forms stable double strands by normal base pairing. Jesse Chen and co-authors tested enzyme-driven building of GNA. Their PLOS ONE paper appeared in 2009. They used DNA templates for the primer-extension work.

GNA interests scientists who study life's origins. Its simplicity hints at chemistry from before life. Getting enzymes to extend GNA strands is a real step. It moves toward evolving functional GNA molecules in the lab. The work tests how far nature's copying machinery can stretch.
plos-pone-0005049:
The gut wall must keep germs out while letting nutrients in. That tightrope is called barrier function. Yutao Yan and colleagues studied a protein that helps control it. Their PLOS ONE paper appeared in 2009. The protein is SPAK, a kinase switched on by salty conditions. Its known jobs included cell differentiation and chloride transport.

SPAK's role in intestinal inflammation was largely unknown. The team found its gene is regulated by hyperosmolarity. SPAK proved involved in the gut's barrier function. The finding links a salt-sensing switch to intestinal disease. A leaky barrier is a hallmark of gut inflammation. SPAK may be one of its controllers.
plos-pone-0005149:
Blood vessels must stay sealed and alive. Cells lining them, endothelial cells, maintain that seal. Signals from neighboring pericytes help stabilize vessels. Tony Walshe and colleagues tested one signal's necessity in PLOS ONE in 2009. The signal is TGF-beta. Their earlier work showed it stabilizing vessels in dishes.

TGF-beta proved required for the adult microvasculature. Without it, the vascular barrier fails. Endothelial survival and vessel homeostasis fail too. Tiny vessels suffer first and worst. The finding names a master keeper of the vasculature. Leaky vessels appear in many diseases, from sepsis to diabetes. Knowing what holds the seal suggests how to repair it. The study moves a dish observation into living tissue.
plos-pone-0005249:
When cells divide, chromosomes are usually pulled apart by spindle fibers gripped at kinetochores. Egg cells build their spindles differently from ordinary dividing cells, though. Deng and colleagues reported a surprise in mouse eggs in PLOS ONE in 2009.

During the second meiotic division, chromosomes moved toward the poles even without kinetochore control. A backup route for moving chromosomes exists in these cells. The finding revises a textbook rule of cell division and may help explain errors that lead to abnormal egg cells. Egg cells must split their genes with great care, since one small slip can end a pregnancy or leave a child with the wrong gene count.
plos-pone-0005349:
Mycobacterium tuberculosis infects about a third of the world's people. Active disease involves fast-growing bacteria, while latent infection involves slow or non-growing ones. Beste and colleagues mapped the genes needed for each growth mode in PLOS ONE in 2009.

The genetic requirements for fast and slow growth differ, as separate gene sets keep each state alive. Drugs that kill fast growers may miss the latent reservoir entirely. Knowing the slow-growth gene list gives drug hunters targets against the hidden form of TB. Most TB drugs were found by their kill of fast-growing germs in a dish. So the slow set has long been a blind spot that this gene list at last brings into view.
plos-pone-0005949:
Inherited changes in one gene form the most common known genetic cause of Parkinson's disease. The gene is LRRK2, and Xiaodong Ding and Matthew Goldberg studied how the cell controls its protein in 2009. Their PLOS ONE paper asks what keeps LRRK2 levels steady, since the protein's exact day job is still unclear.

An enzyme called CHIP, which tags worn proteins for disposal, turns out to govern how stable LRRK2 is. A disposal route of this kind gives drug hunters a new handle on a key Parkinson's protein. If LRRK2 levels can be trimmed safely, that approach could one day sit beside drugs that only block the protein's action.
plos-pone-0006049:
Tbx1 is a gene best known for its link to DiGeorge syndrome, a birth condition affecting the heart and face. Gabriella Fulcoli, Tuong Huynh, Peter Scambler and colleagues found the gene doing unexpected work in 2009. Their PLOS ONE paper shows Tbx1 binding Smad1, a signal carrier in the BMP pathway that patterns the growing body.

The surprise is the manner: Tbx1 damps the BMP-Smad1 signal without acting as a transcription factor, its usual trade. A gene with a second, quieter job helps explain why its loss causes such a wide pattern of defects. The result also adds a new kind of control to a pathway that guides bone, heart and much more.
plos-pone-0006149:
Hantaviruses were long thought to belong to rodents alone, until shrews broke the story. Hae Ji Kang, Shannon Bennett, Laarni Sumibcay and colleagues added a mole to the plot in 2009. Their PLOS ONE paper reports a genetically divergent hantavirus harbored by the European common mole, and reads what it reveals about the family's evolution.

A virus far from the known branches, in a host outside the rodent order, pushes the family's roots deeper and wider. Each new host redraws the map of where hantaviruses hide, which matters since some cause severe human disease. The mole virus is a clue that the family's true host range is still being discovered.
plos-pone-0006249:
